title: Figma Motion — Native Timeline Animation in Figma Design
content:
Figma Motion (introduced at Config 2026, currently OPEN BETA) adds a real animation timeline to Figma Design. It is a different tool from prototyping and solves a different problem.

PROTOTYPING answers 'what happens when the user does this?' — it is interaction-driven, frame-to-frame, and its animation model is a single transition with one duration and one easing.

FIGMA MOTION answers 'how exactly does this move?' — it is time-driven, keyframe-based, and lets multiple properties on multiple layers animate independently along a shared timeline with per-keyframe easing.

HOW TO ENTER IT: click the Motion button in the toolbar. If it is not there, you lack `can edit` access on the file.

WHAT APPEARS: a timeline UI along the bottom of the screen where you set keyframes, adjust animation placement and length, scrub, and preview.

FOUR WAYS TO CREATE AN ANIMATION:
1. PRESET animation styles — Fade, Rotate, Scale, Resize and more, applied without touching keyframes.
2. MANUAL KEYFRAMES — precise control over each layer and property.
3. AUTO-KEYFRAMING — enable it and Figma records every change you make while the playhead moves.
4. THE FIGMA AGENT — describe the motion in words and it generates real keyframes, grounded in your components and tokens.

BETA CAVEAT: features may change and performance issues are expected. Do not make it load-bearing for a deadline without a fallback.

title: The Motion Timeline — Mechanics
content:
THE PLAYHEAD scrubs to any moment. Whatever is on canvas reflects the state at that time, so you design at a moment rather than in the abstract.

LAYERS ON THE TIMELINE: each animated layer gets a track. Drag a layer's bar to shift WHEN it animates; drag its edges to change HOW LONG. This is how you build stagger — offset each layer's bar by 30–50ms instead of chaining frames with After delay.

KEYFRAMES mark a property's value at a point in time. Figma Motion keyframes POSITION, SCALE, ROTATION and OPACITY independently, so one layer can move on one schedule and fade on another. The Plugin API's keyframe fields also cover indexed collections — fills, strokes, effects — so colour and effect animation is keyframeable too.

TIMELINE DURATION is a property of the timeline itself, adjustable (and settable via the API with `setTimelineDuration`).

AUTO-KEYFRAME records changes as you make them with the playhead in motion. Fast for exploration; leaves messy extra keyframes you should clean up afterwards.

STACKING VS SEQUENCING ANIMATION STYLES: styles placed at the same timeline position play together; dragged apart, they sequence. A 'card enters' animation is typically Fade + Move stacked, then a Scale on the icon sequenced 80ms later.

TIME-BASED COMMENTS: collaborators can pin a comment to a specific moment on the timeline. This is the feature that makes motion reviewable asynchronously — 'the overshoot at 0.4s is too much' lands on the exact frame instead of in a Slack thread.

title: Animation Styles — Motion as a Reusable Style
content:
ANIMATION STYLES are Figma Motion's preset animations: Fade, Rotate, Scale, Resize and others. Apply one to a layer and it lands on the timeline as an editable block with its own duration, offset, and properties.

WHY THEY MATTER MORE THAN THEY LOOK: an animation style is a STYLE in the Figma sense — the same category of object as a fill style or a text style. That means motion becomes a shared, named, governed decision rather than a value re-typed per component. Custom animation styles (build and save your own motion library) are announced as coming.

STACK OR SEQUENCE: multiple styles on one layer at the same timeline position play simultaneously; offset them and they sequence. Most real entrances are Fade + Move stacked.

ANIMATED COMPONENTS: turn an animation into a component and reuse it. Motion travels with the component across files and team members the same way fills and typography do. This is the mechanism that makes a motion SYSTEM enforceable rather than aspirational — your 'toast enters' animation is one object, and changing it changes every toast.

MOTION VARIABLES: variables with multiple modes can drive easing and timing. Switching the mode at page level updates every animation that references it, instantly, across the file. That gives you:
- a reduced-motion mode that flattens durations toward zero,
- a brand-specific motion personality per mode,
- a 'demo' mode with slower durations for presentations.

DESIGN SYSTEM CONSEQUENCE: duration and easing stop being numbers in a spec document and become tokens in the file, bound to real animations, versioned with the library. Build the motion token collection before you animate anything, exactly as you would build colour tokens before you paint anything.

title: Figma Motion or Prototyping? A Decision Rule
content:
USE PROTOTYPING when the question is about FLOW AND INTERACTION: what does this button do, where does it go, what state changes, can the user complete the task. Frame-to-frame, triggered by the user, testable with participants.

USE FIGMA MOTION when the question is about TIMING AND FEEL: how does this move, in what order, with what overshoot, over how long. Time-based, authored, reviewable frame by frame.

CONCRETE SPLIT:
- 'Does the checkout flow work?' → prototyping.
- 'Does the add-to-cart confirmation feel good?' → Motion.
- 'Can users find the filter?' → prototyping.
- 'How do the six filter chips stagger in?' → Motion.
- 'What happens when the transaction fails?' → prototyping.
- 'How does the pending→confirmed state transition animate?' → Motion.

WHY YOU NEED BOTH: Smart animate gives you one duration and one easing for an entire transition. Any real animation has multiple elements on different schedules with different curves — that is a timeline, not a transition. Conversely, Motion has no triggers and no branching; it cannot express a flow.

THE PRACTICAL WORKFLOW: prototype the flow first to settle structure, then author the two or three moments that carry the product's character in Motion, then hand off the prototype for logic and the Motion timeline for values.

WHAT MOTION REPLACES: After Effects and Lottie round-trips for UI micro-animation, GIF placeholders in prototypes, and the 'motion spec' Google Doc where durations went to die.

title: Figma Motion — Export and Developer Handoff
content:
EXPORT FORMATS from the file: MP4, GIF, SVG, WEBM. Use MP4 or WEBM for stakeholder review and Slack, GIF only when the destination cannot play video, SVG for genuinely vector animation.

DEV MODE: a MOTION TAB shows the full timeline, read-only and inspectable. Developers scrub it, read exact keyframe times, and copy animation code directly as:
- CSS
- JSON
- React / motion.dev
No interpretation, no 'about 300ms, ease-out-ish'.

MCP SERVER: Figma's Model Context Protocol server exposes full animation context to coding agents from a shareable link. In practice this means an agent implementing your design can read the real keyframes rather than inventing them. Pair it with the `figma-implement-motion` workflow when translating Motion into application code.

WHY THIS CHANGES HANDOFF: the historical failure mode of motion design is that the spec is prose and the build is a guess. An inspectable timeline plus copyable code removes the translation step where fidelity was always lost. The remaining designer job is to say what the code cannot: what should NOT animate, what happens under reduced-motion, and what is interruptible.

WHAT STILL NEEDS WRITING DOWN:
- The reduced-motion variant (Motion's variable modes can express it; say which mode is the reduced one).
- Interruption behaviour — does a dismissal reverse from the current position or queue?
- Performance budget — which properties are permitted (transform and opacity are cheap; width, height, top, left, box-shadow and filter are not).
- Whether the animation is decorative or informational, which determines whether it can be removed.

title: Figma Motion Plugin API — Automating Animation
content:
The Plugin API can read and write Motion data (BETA — subject to change). Relevant when scripting motion through `figma_execute` or building a motion audit.

`figma.motion` NAMESPACE:
- `playheadPosition: number | undefined` (readonly) — current playhead position of the Motion timeline, in seconds.
- `figmaAnimationStyles(): AvailableAnimationStyle[]` — the animation styles available in the current document. Each describes a preset template with configurable `props`, applicable via `applyAnimationStyle`.
- `physicalSpringToNormalized(spring: PhysicalSpring): number` — converts physical spring parameters (stiffness/damping/mass) into Motion's normalised `bounce` value, 0–1.

NODE METHODS:
- `applyAnimationStyle(...)` — applies an animation style to a node; returns the applied animation style instance id.
- `removeAnimationStyle(...)` — removes one.
- `applyManualKeyframeTrack(...)` — applies or REPLACES a manual keyframe track on a node.
- `setTimelineDuration(...)` — updates a timeline's duration.

KEY TYPES:
- `MotionEasing` — `'EASE_IN' | 'EASE_OUT' | 'LINEAR' | 'CUSTOM_CUBIC_BEZIER' | 'CUSTOM_SPRING' | 'HOLD'`. Custom spring uses the normalised `bounce` value.
- `Timeline` — `{ id, duration }`, duration in seconds.
- `ManualKeyframeInput` — `{ timelinePosition (seconds), easing?, value }`.
- `KeyframeField` — the animated property: `'ROTATION'`, `'SCALE_XY'`, `'OPACITY'`, plus indexed collections for fills, strokes and effects.
- `KeyframeValue` — `FLOAT`, `COLOR` (RGBA), `TEXT_DATA`, `VECTOR`, `BOOL`, `CIRCLE`, `LINE`, and point variants (`CIRCLE_POINT`, `COLOR_POINT`).
- `ManualKeyframeTracks` — keyframes organised by property field, with nesting for fills/strokes/effects.
- `AppliedAnimationStyle` — `{ duration, timelineOffset, ...propertyValues }`.

USE CASES: apply one entrance animation across 40 components at once; audit a file for animations exceeding a duration budget; generate a stagger by programmatically offsetting `timelineOffset` per layer; convert an engineering spring spec into Motion's bounce value.

title: Authoring an Animation in Figma Motion — Practical Order
content:
1. FINISH THE STATIC DESIGN FIRST. Animating an unresolved layout means re-animating it. Motion is the last 10% of a screen, not the first.

2. DECIDE WHAT THE MOTION IS SAYING. One sentence: 'the sheet comes from where the button was tapped', 'the confirmation lands with weight because money moved'. If you cannot write the sentence, skip the animation.

3. SET THE TIMELINE DURATION to your target total before you author anything. Working inside a 400ms budget produces different, better decisions than authoring freely and trimming later.

4. ANIMATE THE LEAD ELEMENT ONLY. Get the one important thing right — its properties, its easing, its timing — before touching anything else.

5. ADD SUPPORTING ELEMENTS AS OFFSETS. Drag their bars 30–50ms after the lead. Do not give them their own personality; they share the lead's easing.

6. SCRUB, DON'T PLAY. Playing repeatedly numbs you to the animation. Scrub slowly through the first 100ms and the last 100ms — that is where the problems are: a pop at the start, a hard stop at the end.

7. CHECK THE EXIT. Author it explicitly. Most animations are built as entrances and ship with a default exit that contradicts them.

8. CLEAN UP AUTO-KEYFRAMES. Auto-keyframing leaves redundant keyframes that make the timeline unreadable and the exported code noisy.

9. PROMOTE TO AN ANIMATED COMPONENT once it is right, so it is reused rather than re-authored.

10. WRITE THE REDUCED-MOTION VARIANT as a variable mode, and say in handoff which mode it is.

title: Using the Figma Agent for Motion
content:
Figma's agent can generate real keyframes from a natural-language description of the motion, grounded in your components and tokens (paid plans).

WHERE IT GENUINELY HELPS:
- The repetitive pass. 'Stagger these twelve list items by 40ms with a fade and 8px rise' is a minute of prompting versus twenty minutes of dragging.
- A starting point when you know the feel but not the parameters. 'Make this toast land like a Quick spring' gets you keyframes to refine rather than a blank timeline.
- Consistency work. 'Apply the same entrance as the card component to these four sections.'
- Translating an engineering spec into Motion. 'Duration 240ms, cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1), opacity 0→1 and translateY 12px→0.'

WHERE IT DOES NOT HELP:
- Deciding WHETHER to animate. That is a design judgement about whether the motion carries information, and it is the decision that matters most.
- Character. The two or three moments that define how a product feels are worth authoring by hand; generated motion converges on competent and generic.
- Restraint. An agent asked to make something feel alive will add motion. The better answer is frequently less.

HOW TO USE IT WELL: write the prompt as a spec, not a vibe. Name the properties, the durations, the easing, the stagger. You are using it as a fast executor of a decision you have already made — which is the same relationship you should have with any generation tool in a design workflow.

THEN REVIEW IT the way you would review a junior's work: scrub the first and last 100ms, check the exit, check the reduced-motion mode, check nothing animates that should not.

title: Motion and Interaction in Figma Sites
content:
Figma Sites (open beta since Config 2025) publishes real websites from Figma and carries interaction types that do not exist in Figma Design. Relevant when the deliverable is a marketing site or landing page.

INHERITED FROM FIGMA DESIGN: Change to, Back, Scroll to, plus page-to-page Links.

SITES-ONLY INTERACTIONS:
- REVEAL — makes elements visible on a trigger such as entering the viewport or page load. This is the scroll-reveal pattern, built in.
- SCROLL TRANSFORM — ties an element's size, position, opacity and rotation to scroll progress. This is how you build scroll-driven hero effects, progress indicators, and pinned sections.
- PARALLAX — shifts elements in response to CURSOR movement for depth.
- MARQUEE — continuous scrolling of elements. Settings: direction, speed in pixels per second, and whether it loops infinitely.
- DRAGGABLE — users click and drag elements around.
- LIGHTBOX — an overlay that expands the selected element into a full-screen modal with a dimmed background.
- CURSOR EFFECTS — replaces the mouse cursor with an image, vector, or frame.

SCROLL TO ANIMATION OPTIONS: Instant (jump) or Animate (the page scrolls to the target).

JUDGEMENT: these are the exact effects that make an agency site feel considered and a product site feel slow. Scroll transform and Reveal on above-the-fold content delay comprehension and hurt LCP. Marquee and cursor effects are brand statements with a real accessibility cost — both should respect reduced-motion, and a custom cursor removes an affordance users rely on. Use one signature effect per site, not seven.
source: help.figma.com — Figma Sites collection: Add interactions to a website

title: Reviewing Motion — What to Look For
content:
Reviewing animation is a distinct skill from reviewing layout, and 'it looks nice' is not a review.

SCRUB THE FIRST 100MS. Almost every bad animation is bad at the start: an element pops in at full opacity before moving, a scale begins from 0 and looks like a glitch, something appears one frame before its siblings for no reason.

SCRUB THE LAST 100MS. The second failure zone: a hard stop with no deceleration, an overshoot that never settles, an element still moving after the content is readable.

COUNT THE MOVING THINGS. More than three independent motions in one transition has no focal point. Ask which one is the lead; if nobody can answer, the choreography is missing.

CHECK THE EXIT EXISTS. Ask to see the dismissal. Roughly half of reviewed animations have never had their exit authored.

TIME IT AGAINST THE TASK. Multiply the duration by how many times a day the user will see it. 400ms × 60 times is 24 seconds a day spent watching your animation.

TEST ON THE WORST DEVICE YOU SUPPORT. Smooth in Figma tells you nothing. Motion that janks is worse than no motion, because jank reads as brokenness.

ASK FOR THE REDUCED-MOTION VERSION. If it does not exist, the work is not finished. Vestibular disorders are not an edge case.

ASK WHAT IT COMMUNICATES. If the answer is 'it makes it feel more premium', push once: what specifically does the user learn from this movement? A good answer names a relationship — origin, causality, identity, or status. No answer means it is decoration, which is allowed once per surface and not more.
